title: "A tool for valuing contributions in teams"
author: "Owen Petchey"

Working in teams can be some of the most stimulating, exciting, and important experiences we have. At other times things can get a bit sticky — for example when it comes to attributing rewards, such as deciding authorship and authorship order on publications. Proactive planning and assessment of contributions can help, alongside a collaboration agreement.

The [web application for valuing contributions in teams](https://owenpetchey.shinyapps.io/valuing_contributions_in_teams/) summarises the contributions a team can report in the associated [Google Sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1jw3rfSDpQbT-IfgGsCbYSy7XIe92UiZqCFw8zMZcLRM). Below is a bit more detail about the problems it addresses and how.

### In the Google Sheet, you:

- Enter the project information you have so far; update as required.
- Enter your team members by name.
- Enter the contributions made by each team member on the contributions sheet.

### Problems and solutions in team projects

There are a number of recurring challenges:

- Authorship order alone doesn't capture what are, in reality, nuanced, continuous, and diverse types of contribution.
- Lack of transparency in team members' efforts can lead to [overestimating our own contribution and underestimating others'](https://www.thecut.com/2017/04/what-to-do-when-you-feel-like-the-only-roommate-who-cleans.html).
- Contributions change over the course of a project.
- Actual and intended contributions can diverge.
- Value created by synergies is hard to account for.

Some solutions to these problems:

- Use the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) with a degree of contribution (lead, equal, supporting), and report this in publications.
- Keep a team-accessible list of contributions.
- Track how contributions evolve, from intended to actual/final.
- Use a transparent, flexible method for translating actual/final contributions into authorship order.
- Give each contributor responsibility for recording their own contributions.
- Give the project leader responsibility for making sure this self-responsibility is understood, remembered, and acted upon — e.g. by building it into the team's research culture, and issuing reminders.
